content.title: Supreme Court Updates: Key Justices Appear Skeptical of Limiting Birthright Citizenship
content.text: Here are five takeaways from the birthright citizenship argument at the Supreme Court.VideoKey Justices Appear Skeptical of Limiting Birthright CitizenshipDuring a Supreme Court hearing on Wednesday, several justices expressed skepticism about the Trump administration’s efforts to bar children of undocumented immigrants born in the United States from automatically becoming Americans.CreditCredit...Anna Rose Layden for The New York TimesMembers of the Supreme Court’s conservative majority peppered the Trump administration’s top appellate lawyer with probing questions at Wednesday’s argument over the president’s efforts to revise the longstanding understanding of birthright citizenship.Minutes into the session, which was attended by President Trump, Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. called a key aspect of the administration’s position “very quirky” — perhaps not a great sign for Mr. Trump’s position. But the case did not appear to be a clear-cut rout, with the justices lobbing challenging inquiries to both sides.Here is a look at some of the telling exchanges.The justices wanted to understand better what ‘domicile’ means and why it matters to the case.The administration is not asking the Supreme Court to overturn its 1898 precedent in Wong Kim Ark, in which the court ruled a child born in San Francisco to Chinese parents was a citizen. But key to its argument to limit birthright citizenship is the fact that Mr. Wong’s parents were legal permanent residents — or “domiciled” — in the United States.D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, told the court that because illegal immigrants and temporary visitors are not “domiciled” here, their newborn babies are not citizens, meaning the court could side with him and not overturn the precedent.At least five justices asked questions about numerous references to domicile in the 1898 ruling. Was that reference part of why the court ruled then for Mr. Wong? Or was it just a neutral recitation of the circumstances of the people involved? The former would make the distinction legally significant. The latter would be an aside.“Isn’t it at least something to be concerned about, to say that since it is discussed 20 different times and has that significant role in the opinion, that you can just dismiss it as irrelevant?” Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who is often in the majority in major decisions, asked Cecillia Wang, the lawyer who argued on behalf of people challenging Mr. Trump’s order.“What are those 20 domicile words doing there?” added Justice Elena Kagan. “Like, why did they sprinkle that in the opinion?”In response, Ms. Wang said the ruling was just summarizing the stipulated facts of the case. The more critical takeaway from the decision, she argued, was it reaffirmed the clear purpose of the 14th Amendment, which she said was a universal rule of birthright citizenship with very limited exceptions.On the flip side, Justice Neil M. Gorsuch and Justice Kagan pressed the solicitor general about the absence of the word “domicile” in the 19th century debates surrounding the adoption of the 14th Amendment. Justice Gorsuch noted that there was no mention of the citizenship or residency status of parents, but rather a focus on newborn children.“In none of the debates do we have parents discussed,” the justice said. “And you don’t see domicile mentioned in the debates. The absence is striking.”If the court allows the order, it’s not clear the ruling would apply only to babies not yet born.“This executive order applies only prospectively,” Mr. Sauer said, “and we ask the court to rule only prospectively.”Justice Sonia Sotomayor was skeptical. “You asked us to concentrate only on the prospective nature of the executive order, but the logic of your position, if accepted, is that this president, or the next president, or a Congress, or someone else, could decide that it shouldn’t be prospective,” she said. “There would be nothing limiting that, according to your theory.”That was an echo of a point made in a friend-of-the-court brief from more than 200 Democratic members of Congress, which said the president was powerless to declare that a constitutional provision or federal law applied only in the future. After all, if the Constitution and the federal law do not grant birthright citizenship, countless people never acquired it.“Should the court endorse the administration’s interpretations,” the brief said, “millions of Americans will simply no longer meet the constitutional and statutory criteria for citizenship. Statutory law will therefore bar them from voting, securing passports, and more.”Justice Barrett seemed concerned about practical issues, including foundlings.Justice Amy Coney Barrett said the administration’s position could be “messy in some applications,” giving the example of foundlings — babies abandoned soon after birth whose parents are unknown.“What if you don’t know who the parents are?” she asked. Would that deprive an infant of U.S. citizenship?Mr. Sauer pointed to a 1952 law that conferred citizenship on children of “unknown parentage” under the age of 5 who were found in the United States unless it was proved, before they turned 21, that they had not been born in the United States. (Notably, the law did not exclude children later shown to have been born to people in the United States temporarily or unlawfully.)But Justice Barrett was not satisfied with that answer. “Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah,” she said. “But what about the Constitution?”Mr. Sauer did not give a direct answer, which suggested that under his interpretation of the 14th Amendment, foundlings could be stateless.Key justices are not interested in the policy debates.In making the case to limit birthright citizenship, the Trump administration raised several policy concerns. First, that the nation’s longstanding practice has incentivized foreigners, including from hostile nations, to travel to the United States to have babies. The administration asserts so-called birth tourism is a national security threat. Second, it argued that many other countries, particularly in Europe, do not grant automatic birthright citizenship.But key justices suggested those policy concerns should play no role in the outcome of the case, which should focus on the law and Constitution.After asking Mr. Sauer about how significant a problem birth tourism is, Chief Justice Roberts asked:“Having said all that, you do agree that that has no impact on the legal analysis before us?”Mr. Sauer acknowledged that birth tourism was not a problem in the 19th century, which is to say, it was not an issue that people considered when they drafted the 14th Amendment. But, he said, “we’re in a new world now,” where 8 billion people are a plane ride away from having a child, who is a U.S. citizen.“Well, it’s a new world. It’s the same Constitution,” the chief justice quipped.Similarly, Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh, who mostly asked open-ended questions that did not telegraph how he might vote, was skeptical of the administration’s arguments about the practices of other nations being at odds with the history of birthright citizenship in the United States.He called that argument a “very good point” as a policy matter. But he said the court’s role is to try to “interpret American law with American precedent based on American history.”“I guess, I’m not seeing the relevance as a legal, constitutional interpretive matter,” he added.There are at least two ways Trump could lose.By the conclusion of the argument, it seemed clear that it would be easier for the court, if only as a practical matter, to rule against the administration.Justice Kavanaugh sketched out two possible decisions along those lines. One would simply say that the 1898 precedent supports the challengers’ interpretation of the 14th Amendment.Justice Kavanaugh noted that Mr. Sauer had not asked the court to overrule the decision. “That could just be a short opinion, right?” he asked Ms. Wang. She was quick to agree.A second way to rule against the administration, the justice said, would be to avoid the Constitution entirely and focus on a 1952 federal law that independently guarantees birthright citizenship. “Our usual practice, as you’re well aware, of course, is to resolve things on statutory grounds and not to do a constitutional ground,” Justice Kavanaugh told Ms. Wang.That also sounded good to her. “We obviously have these two paths to a win here,” she said. “We’re happy to win on either or both of them.”Mr. Sauer had already indicated that if he had to lose, he would rather do so based on the statute. That would allow the administration to seek new legislation. If Congress tried to limit birthright citizenship explicitly, that would prompt another round of litigation.April 1, 2026Miriam Jordan and Zach MontagueMiriam Jordan and Zach Montague were at the Supreme Court for the birthright citizenship arguments.Immigrant families watched the Supreme Court case with cautious hope.ImageMaria and Francisco Andreote are Brazilian microbiologists conducting research at Penn State. Their daughter, Laura, 4, was born in the United States just before the birthright citizenship case landed in the Supreme Court.Credit...via the Andreote familyImmigrants and children of immigrants expressed cautious hope on Wednesday after the Supreme Court heard arguments on whether there should be limits on universal birthright citizenship. Many noted how the justices appeared skeptical of Mr. Trump’s executive order to end the right.“We are relieved, and it makes us feel more secure that we belong here and are appreciated here,” said Maria Brossi Andreote, a microbiologist from Brazil who came to the United States in 2019 on a temporary visa who spoke by phone from Pennsylvania.Many immigrants were unwilling to talk or share their full name, fearing that remarks perceived as critical of the government could undermine their ability to remain in the country. But amid the uncertainty, they were encouraged by the debate.Andres and Bea, both Ph.D. candidates from Peru on student visas, were expecting their first baby when Mr. Trump issued his order last year limiting birthright citizenship. They found themselves initially consumed by uncertainty: Would they have to leave the country? What costs would they face? They felt better about their prospects on Wednesday.“If it’s becoming clear they won’t be changing birthright citizenship, we can start making long-term plans, like having more kids,” Andres said, speaking from a university in the Northeast. “You don’t want to put your kids at risk of not having access to a lot of things.”Outside the court under a bright blue sky, many children of immigrants were among the hundreds of people who converged in front of the Supreme Court to show support for preserving birthright citizenship. They waved American flags and held signs that said, “If you are born in the USA, you are an American citizen.”Among the demonstrators was Kevin Xu of Fairfax, Va., whose parents immigrated from China in the 1980s and 1990s.“Birthright citizenship has been the foundation for our community, for the Chinese American community,” he said. “It really shows how the attitude of what the American dream is — what the American dream promises — has really changed.”Richard Benjumea, whose parents immigrated to the United States from Colombia, said, “I’m out here as a son of immigrants, I benefited from birthright citizenship.”But he said the issue extended beyond immigrant communities.“So we’re out here for all the immigrants and pretty much everybody — everybody in the United States — because what starts with the immigrants will eventually catch up to everybody else,” Mr. Benjumea said.The crowd swelled as a succession of speakers, including the celebrity chef and activist José Andrés, addressed the stakes at play between songs by the Puerto Rican star Bad Bunny and other Spanish-language singers that blared out of speakers.The rally was organized by national groups like the American Civil Liberties Union and immigrant advocacy groups including CASA and the League of United Latin American Citizens, whose members handed out hats, signs and water.Some people peeled off to the periphery, following a livestream of the arguments unfolding inside, or cheering from shaded areas.Getúlio González-Mulattieri, 37, a veteran of the U.S. Air Force and an American citizen born in Brazil, traveled from Ithaca, N.Y.“I was born abroad and I would not have been able to contribute if I had not been able to obtain citizenship,” said Mr. González-Mulattieri, a student at Cornell University.He said that he came from a mixed-status family of citizens, lawful immigrants and undocumented immigrants.“I’m here for them,” he said. “These issues hit close to home.”If birthright citizenship ends, some U.S.-born infants would be able to acquire the citizenship of their parents, if their country of origin allows that. However, if born to parents from countries that do not grant citizenship through a parent, the babies could end up stateless.Although few immigrants appeared to be among the people who had come to protest, some followed the news on websites, from their homes or from their workplaces, such as Ms. Andreote and her husband, Francisco Andreote, who is also a microbiologist. Penn State recruited both of them to do government-funded research on crop productivity, and immediately sponsored themfor legal permanent residency, a bureaucratic process that can take years.Before the couple’s green cards were issued in April 2022, including for their older child, now 8, they gave birth to a U.S.-born child, Laura, in January. Under Mr. Trump’s plan, she would have not been granted U.S. citizenship.After the arguments on Wednesday, Ms. Andreote was more confident about her family’s future.“My children are being raised here, English is their first language and we are contributing to this country,” she said.Amy Qin and Aishvarya Kavi contributed reporting.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTTrump was joined in the Supreme Court with White House general counsel David Warrington, according to a White House official.I was in court without my phone, which no one is allowed to carry inside. Some of what I saw during the argument:The solicitor general, John Sauer, appeared to be leading an orchestra. His movements were expansive, both arms cutting through the air as he made the case again and again that foreigners in the country temporarily did not have allegiance to the United States.One of the speakers outside the Supreme Court today was Norman Wong, 76, a direct descendant of Wong Kim Ark, the Chinatown cook who was behind the 1898 case that affirmed birthright citizenship for all. It was not until much later in life that Wong found out about his prominent relative, a measure of how deeply ingrained birthright citizenship has become in the American consciousness and how rarely Wong Kim Ark’s case is taught in schools. “They will be shamed for history if they get this wrong,” Wong said in an interview outside the Court. He attended with his wife.ImageCredit...Amy Qin/The New York Times“I come out of the court today with the thought of my parents and so many of our parents and ancestors,” Cecillia Wang, the A.C.L.U. lawyer who argued before the justices, tells reporters on the steps of the court. “We couldn’t be more confident.”ImageCredit...Anna Rose Layden for The New York TimesAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTWalking outside the Supreme Court among a crowd of demonstrators was John Eastman, a California law professor who was among the first to promote what was then considered the fringe notion that the 14th Amendment does not actually grant citizenship to anyone born in the United States. Eastman said he was highly impressed with the arguments from both sides. “I think it just proves that it’s not a radical fringe idea — that it’s a very significant originalist debate, and we’ll see how the court rules,” he said. Mr. Eastman is also known for drafting a plan to block congressional certification of the 2020 presidential election.ImageCredit...Anna Rose Layden for The New York TimesPresident Trump has issued his first public reaction to the oral arguments on birthright citizenship after he appeared in the Supreme Court for the case. In a post on his social media site, Trump says falsely the United States is the “only Country in the World STUPID enough to allow “Birthright” Citizenship!” In fact, the United States is one of more than 30 countries that confer citizenship at birth with no conditions, according to the Library of Congress.About 13 minutes into the oral arguments by the A.C.L.U. lawyer, Cecillia Wang, President Trump abruptly rose from where he was sitting in the first row of the public section. He departed the courtroom, followed by two escorts.The argument is over. The justices will meet shortly to cast their tentative votes. The decision is likely to land in late June or early July.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe celebrity chef and activist Jose Andrés gave a rousing speech to the crowd outside. “Today is not about defending a constitutional right,” he said.“Today is about so much more: today is about defending the pure idea of what America is and will be.”ImageCredit...Anna Rose Layden for The New York TimesJustice Kavanaugh is asking the A.C.L.U.’s lawyer about possible ways of resolving the case and suggests it could be a short opinion if the justices were to uphold Wong Kim Ark and side with the A.C.L.U.VideoCreditCredit...U.S. Supreme Court Didn’t the Supreme Court already hear this case?ImageProtesters in favor of birthright citizenship outside the Supreme Court in May.Credit...Haiyun Jiang for The New York TimesIf this case sounds familiar, that might be because the Supreme Court has already ruled on one aspect of litigation over President Trump’s executive order ending the guarantee of birthright citizenship.But importantly, that case did not test the constitutionality of the order itself, as the one the justices are hearing on Wednesday will do.When Mr. Trump issued the executive order in January 2025, it was immediately challenged by Democratic-led states and immigrant advocacy groups, which said it would lead to chaos and uncertainty for parents who would have to prove their immigration status for their babies to be citizens.The order was quickly blocked by lower court judges who said it was at odds with the 14th Amendment. The judges issued what are called universal injunctions, blocking the order for the whole country and not just for the parties that sued.Such injunctions have been controversial, with presidents of both parties questioning whether lower court judges should have the power to issue such sweeping blocks of policies while their legality is being challenged.In response to an emergency request from the administration, the justices agreed in May to consider only the question of whether a judge was right to issue such a nationwide injunction to block the executive order — and in general whether nationwide orders are legal.In a 6-to-3 ruling in June, the Supreme Court sided with the administration, limiting the ability of individual lower court judges to issue universal orders, saying they most likely exceeded the authority Congress has given the federal courts.The court’s liberal justices dissented, warning of an endlessly confusing environment in which people or groups could be forced to file individual lawsuits to advocate a child’s citizenship as each baby is born.At the time, the justices paused their decision for at least 30 days to prevent the birthright citizenship order from immediately going into effect. They also left open a path for additional challenges using a different legal tool known as a class action, in which a single lawsuit is filed on behalf of a set of similarly situated people.Indeed, class-action lawsuits challenging the birthright citizenship order quickly followed. One was the case the justices are hearing on Wednesday, which was filed in New Hampshire on behalf of a group of expectant parents and their children who would be subject to the order. The lower court judge, Joseph N. Laplante, certified the lawsuit as a class action and blocked the administration’s order in July. His decision has applied nationwide to the babies of undocumented parents.Judge Laplante said in his ruling that citizenship was the most foundational benefit the government could extend.“It is the greatest privilege that exists in the world,” he said.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTIn the demonstrations outside the Supreme Court, Maria Jose said she was born a citizen in Ponce, Puerto Rico. But even so, she said she felt there were segments of the country that do not recognize her as an American. “I can look around my Spanish community and my Spanish heritage, and I see how much they’re suffering through the immigration issue, and I see how much other communities are suffering the same as me,” she said.She said she was heartened by how many people from many different backgrounds had turned out on Tuesday, and felt undeterred by Trump being just inside the building.“Perhaps what he was trying to do is separate us, but here we are united,” she said. “So the climate, I see it as positive, although we are having some issues, we are now united.”ImageCredit...Anna Rose Layden for The New York TimesIn the first part of the argument, John Sauer, the administration’s lawyer, faced skeptical questions from key justices, but it wasn’t a rout. In the second part, some of those same justices vigorously probed the position of the A.C.L.U.’s lawyer, Cecillia Wang.We’ve entered the second phase of Wang’s argument, where she faces one-by-one questions from the justices, in descending order of seniority.April 1, 2026Anna Rose LaydenDemonstrators gather at the Supreme Court as oral arguments are heard on birthright citizenship.Anna Rose Layden for The New York TimesAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTPresident Trump departed the Supreme Court oral arguments at the end of Solicitor General Sauer’s arguments and is now back at the White House.ImageCredit...Jonathan Ernst/ReutersAt least five justices have addressed the question of whether multiple references to “domicile” in a key 1898 precedent were part of its holding or just a neutral recitation of the circumstances of the people involved in it. The former would make the distinction legally significant. The latter would be an aside.Outside of the court, Kevin Xu of Fairfax, Va., said his parents came to the United States from China as part of a wave during the 1980s and 1990s.“Birthright citizenship has been the foundation for our community, for the Chinese American community,” he said. “It really shows how the attitude of what the American dream is — what the what the American dream promises — has really changed,” Xu said. When his parents arrived in the 1990s, he said, the attitude was people should just work hard and “then you’ll be American like one of us.’” Thirty years later, he said he felt that attitude was changing. “And that is really scary.”Chief Justice Roberts is asking tough questions of both sides. He’s referring to the key 1898 precedent in Wong Kim Ark, which mentions 20 times that Wong’s parents were “domiciled” or had permanent residence in the United States. The chief justice asks the A.C.L.U. attorney if that language can just be dismissed as irrelevant.VideoCreditCredit...U.S. Supreme CourtAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTIn the final question to the solicitor general, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson touched on the practical challenges some parents could face in proving their babies’ citizenship: “Are we bringing women in for depositions? How are we figuring this out?”VideoCreditCredit...U.S. Supreme Court After more than an hour of arguments from the Trump administration, Cecillia Wang, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union, is presenting arguments on behalf of a class of people challenging the executive order curtailing birthright citizenship. She is a birthright citizen herself.Under Trump’s approach, foundlings given up for adoption could be stateless.ImageA 9-month-old girl who was born in the United States to Afghan immigrants having her photo taken for her U.S. passport.Credit...Todd Heisler/The New York TimesFive years ago, when the Supreme Court heard arguments over whether it should overrule Roe v. Wade, Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked a series of questions about safe haven laws, which allow parents to anonymously surrender newborn babies at hospitals or firehouses, without fear of prosecution.Her point was that the laws eased some of the burdens of what she called “forced motherhood,” even in absence of a right to abortion. But if President Trump prevails in the birthright citizenship case, a mother contemplating taking such a step may want to consider another factor: Would her baby be a U.S. citizen?Under Mr. Trump’s executive order, abandoned infants would not be entitled to citizenship under the 14th Amendment unless they were able to produce evidence that at least one of their biological parents was a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident. That would seem to leave parents seeking to invoke safe haven laws with a terrible choice, one that could leave their children stateless.A 1952 law addressed this problem, though it is not clear whether it would survive a ruling in favor of Mr. Trump’s plan. The law conferred citizenship on children of “unknown parentage” under the age of 5 who were found in the United States unless it was proved, before they turned 21, that they had not been born in the United States.Notably, the law did not exclude children later shown to have been born to people in the United States temporarily or unlawfully.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTJustice Barrett says the administration’s reading of the 14th Amendment introduces “a new kind of citizenship.” She suggests people might have made a bigger deal of this during the debates over the 14th Amendment after the Civil War if it were true.Lawful Asian immigrants would be disproportionately affected if birthright citizenship ends.ImageDemonstrators outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday.Credit...Anna Rose Layden for The New York TimesIf President Trump succeeds in eliminating universal birthright citizenship, there could be 6.4 million U.S.-born children without legal status by 2050, according to a new study.In addition to affecting undocumented immigrants in the country, the authors say, that change would have a disproportionate effect on Asians who are in the country lawfully.The Supreme Court is hearing arguments on Wednesday over Mr. Trump’s executive order to deny U.S. citizenship to children born in the country to undocumented immigrants and to those born to foreign nationals in the country lawfully on temporary visas. His plan, if upheld by the court, would reinterpret the 14th Amendment of the Constitution.The largest number of people affected would be Hispanics, according to the study, which was conducted by Penn State scholars who research immigration. Latinos make up the largest undocumented group in the United States, and Hispanic babies would account for eight out of 10 people born in the country but not considered American citizens by 2050.However, the biggest relative change in births of babies without citizenship would be among Asians, at 41 per 1,000 Asian immigrants. That compares with 17 births of children without citizenship per 1,000 undocumented Latinos, according to the authors of the study.“For Latinos, we would see the most growth in absolute numbers of undocumented people,” said Jennifer Van Hook, a demographer who is a co-author of the study, which was based on analysis of census data and immigration records.“But relative to the small size of the undocumented Asian population, we would see very high numbers of Asian children born in the U.S. without citizenship,” she said. “We would be creating an undocumented population of Asians out of thin air.”Many of the children would be born to parents from countries such as India and China who are in the United States on student or work visas. Under Mr. Trump’s executive order, they would no longer be U.S. citizens.About half the people in the country on temporary student and work visas eventually obtain legal permanent residency, which puts them on the path to American citizenship. If birthright citizenship is eliminated, their children would have no such path.Most of them have been working and paying taxes in the United States for years and are in their prime childbearing years. And many have been waiting in a backlog for more than a decade to obtain permanent legal residency through their employer. Often, they have already had children born in the United States who have the full rights of citizenry.“This executive order would generate mixed-status families for Asians, where parents are here legally waiting for green cards and would have children akin to undocumented,” said Nicole Kriesberg, who is an assistant professor of public policy at Penn State and an author of the study.“The U.S. would be recruiting people for these visas and depriving their children of citizenship,” she said.The United States is among at least 30 countries that automatically grant citizenship to anyone born within its borders. The beneficiaries include the children of foreign nationals in the country on temporary visas, millions of undocumented residents as well as so-called birth tourists, who travel to the United States while pregnant with the objective of having American babies.Of the 51.3 million people in the United States in 2023 who were born in another country, nearly half were citizens, according to a report last year by the Migration Policy Institute. Another 19 percent were lawful permanent residents who could become naturalized citizens. And 5 percent were in the country on student, work or other temporary visas.The remaining 27 percent, or about 13.7 million people, were undocumented.Beyond significantly adding to the undocumented immigrant population, the end of birthright citizenship for many children could create an underclass of U.S.-born children that would stretch across generations, according to the institute’s report.In a brief filed to the Supreme Court, 141 scholars said that research has demonstrated that Mr. Trump’s order would cause “great harm” to the children and their families and communities, as well the U.S. economy. (The Penn State scholars are not part of this group.)“If enforced, the order would dramatically expand the undocumented population of the U.S., destabilizing U.S. communities and labor markets,” they wrote.The argument has included some back and forth over what makes people temporary residents of the United States versus permanent immigrants. The questions are critical. As the Trump administration’s detention and deportation campaign has been initiated, many immigrants have watched the legal ground shift under their feet. Humanitarian and temporary protection programs have been rolled back and hundreds of thousands of people with temporary legal status or limited forms of authorization to be in the country are now subject to deportation.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTForget the 14th Amendment. A 1952 law also takes on birthright citizenship.ImageProtesters outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday.Credit...Anna Rose Layden for The New York TimesIn its Supreme Court briefs, the Trump administration focused almost all of its attention on convincing the justices that the 14th Amendment, which was adopted in 1868 after the Civil War, did not automatically confer citizenship on children born to parents who were in the United States unlawfully or temporarily.The government’s briefs spend considerably less time on the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, which says that anyone “born in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof,” is a citizen.The statute’s language mirrors that of the amendment. D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, has argued that the statute and the constitutional provision must, therefore, mean the same thing. If the 14th Amendment does not confer citizenship on babies born in the United States to parents here unlawfully or temporarily, he said, the statute must not, either. (And, presumably, the other way around.)The challengers and their supporters responded that, whatever might have been the original meaning of the 14th Amendment, there is substantial evidence that Congress understood the 1952 law to guarantee birthright citizenship. They pointed to judicial decisions, legislative reports and executive practice to establish what they said was the consensus view in the middle of the last century.There is no question that Congress has the power to grant citizenship, including birthright citizenship, whatever the correct interpretation of the constitutional amendment. Indeed, Mr. Sauer acknowledged that federal lawmakers could “confer citizenship at birth upon various categories of persons who are not guaranteed citizenship under the 14th Amendment” — and that they did so in several provisions of the 1952 law.The Supreme Court ordinarily does not reach a constitutional question if it can decide a case on statutory grounds, meaning the court could rule against Mr. Trump without ever even considering what the Constitution requires.Should the court rule against the administration based on the 1952 law and leave the meaning of the 14th Amendment unresolved, the administration could choose a new path, asking Congress to adopt legislation to curtail birthright citizenship. Such bills have been introduced, without success, in almost every Congress since 1995.Let’s imagine that Congress did enact a law along the lines of Mr. Trump’s executive order. It would surely be challenged as a violation of the 14th Amendment — and end up right back in front of the justices.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTCan Trump declare that his birthright rules apply only in the future?ImageCredit...Eric Gay/Associated PressPresident Trump’s executive order curtailing birthright citizenship said that it was prospective only, applying to babies born 30 days after it becomes effective. Since the order has been blocked by lower courts, no one has yet been subject to it. Should Mr. Trump win in the Supreme Court, the order will come to life 30 days after the ruling.But it is hardly clear that the president gets to decide when the Constitution counts.In a brief for the challengers, the American Civil Liberties Union said that accepting Mr. Trump’s arguments “would be the beginning, not the end, of a constitutional revolution rippling out in innumerable ways — some of which can be anticipated, others perhaps not.”There is no assurance, the brief said, that a ruling for the administration would only look forward and not also affect the citizenship status of millions of Americans who were born before it was issued.“The order may be formally prospective, applying to tens of thousands of children born every month, and devastating families around the country,” the brief said. “But worse yet, the government’s baseless arguments — if accepted — would cast a shadow over the citizenship of millions upon millions of Americans, going back generations.”A friend-of-the-court brief from more than 200 Democratic members of Congress went further, saying the president was powerless to declare that a constitutional provision or federal law applied only in the future. After all, if the Constitution and the federal law do not grant birthright citizenship, countless people never acquired it.“Should the court endorse the administration’s interpretations,” the brief said, “millions of Americans will simply no longer meet the constitutional and statutory criteria for citizenship. Statutory law will therefore bar them from voting, securing passports and more. The administration cannot change that by announcing that it will (for now) treat those erstwhile Americans as if they were citizens, giving them benefits the law forbids them to have.”AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTExperts say enforcing a limit to birthright citizenship would be costly.ImageThe country’s current system for recording and handling birth records is highly decentralized.Credit...Haiyun Jiang for The New York TimesPresident Trump’s executive order to limit birthright citizenship in the future stipulates that babies born in the United States to undocumented immigrants, and some temporary foreign residents, will no longer be granted citizenship automatically.Verifying citizenship at birth would be costly and difficult, complicated by the likelihood of inaccuracies and incomplete information, according to data scientists, former government officials and lawyers who have worked on citizenship cases.For one thing, the current system for recording and handling vital records in the United States — official legal documents memorializing life events like birth, death, marriage and divorce — is highly decentralized.Registering birth records is the responsibility of the jurisdiction where the event occurred, usually a town or county, according to the National Association for Public Health Statistics and Information Systems, which represents vital records offices in all states and territories, along with New York City and the District of Columbia.Most births occur in hospitals or licensed birth centers, where demographic and medical information about the child and parents is collected, and then sent to the state.Home births, which have increased dramatically and now account for 1.5 percent of all births, typically require a parent to submit documentation to local agencies within a week, sometimes through a manual, paper process. About a quarter of home births are unexpected or happen without a medical professional present, making the process more cumbersome.Parents sometimes delay selecting a name or may be reluctant to fill out the paperwork because of extenuating circumstances or personal beliefs. Failing to register until a year after birth, or even longer, is not unheard of. And family complications — such as questions over surrogacy — portend a “complex mess,” according to a forthcoming article by Scott Titshaw, a law professor at Mercer University.State agencies eventually send the data to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for statistical and health policy purposes. But privacy and confidentiality laws make it very difficult to access those records, said Amy O’Hara, a research professor at Georgetown University’s Massive Data Institute, and a former senior executive at the U.S. Census Bureau.Ambitious federal database initiatives have sometimes been problematic, she cautioned, citing the Treasury Department’s Do Not Pay Initiative to help agencies gain access to databases and verify eligibility before releasing federal funds.
